positions.source_passage: Yes, and for one class of device it is the only comparator that describes reality. For augmentative and alternative communication, the absence of the device is not a slower or less expert version of the same function. It is the absence of the function. There is no unaided clinical judgment to fall back on, because the judgment being aided is the user's own expression, and no clinician can supply it.
positions.position_gist: For devices whose function is the user's own expression (e.g., AAC for nonverbal users), the absence-of-device comparator is the only one that describes the real counterfactual because no human alternative performs the function.

positions.source_passage: Device performance is not bounded below by the no-device baseline. A comparator framework built on panels or standard of care implicitly treats the device as adding some amount of benefit between zero and the expert ceiling. A generative device that fabricates output does not land at zero. It lands below it, because the no-device condition produces no false record and the device does.
positions.position_gist: Panel and standard-of-care comparators wrongly assume device performance is bounded below by zero benefit, whereas fabricated output is worse than no device at all, so comparator frameworks must account for below-baseline performance.

positions.source_passage: Against a panel comparator, a device that produces a plausible but wrong output scores as a partial success. Against the absence comparator, the same output is a categorical harm, because the counterfactual is not a worse sentence. It is no sentence.
positions.position_gist: A panel comparator awards partial credit to plausible-but-fabricated outputs, while the absence comparator correctly treats such outputs as categorical harm.

positions.source_passage: We are not proposing that absence of the device become the primary comparator for GenAI-enabled devices generally. It is a poor instrument for measuring benefit. Against no device at all, almost any functioning system looks excellent, and a sponsor permitted to choose it would be choosing the weakest available bar.
positions.position_gist: The commenter qualifies that the absence comparator should not become the general primary comparator because it sets too weak a bar for measuring benefit.

positions.source_passage: We therefore recommend the absence comparator be used alongside, not instead of, the comparators in Section V.C \u2014 and specifically as a pass/fail gate rather than a scored dimension. A device that produces fabricated output over null input has failed regardless of how well it performs on the panel comparator, because the two results are measuring different things and the good one does not offset the bad one.
positions.position_gist: Recommends the absence comparator be used alongside existing comparators as a pass/fail floor test, with fabricated output over null input constituting failure regardless of panel-comparator performance.

positions.source_passage:
We propose three tests a sponsor can apply to determine whether the absence comparator is required for a given device, and to justify the choice.
 1. Is there a human who performs this function without the device? ... 2. Can the user detect and contest an incorrect output? ... 3. Does an incorrect output leave a durable record attributed to the user? ... A device answering no, no, yes to those three should be evaluated against the absence comparator as a condition of clearance, not as an optional supplementary analysis.
positions.position_gist: Proposes a three-part test (no human performs the function, user cannot detect/contest errors, output leaves a durable record attributed to the user) to determine when the absence comparator should be mandatory as a condition of clearance.

positions.source_passage: The absence comparator is cheap to operationalize for devices that ingest sensor input. The test is to present the device with input containing no valid signal and record whether it produces output. ... Under the absence comparator the acceptance criterion is exact and requires no clinical judgment: output produced from input carrying no signal is a failure, scored as a failure, regardless of how plausible the output is. No panel, no adjudication, no inter-rater reliability. It is fully automatable and it directly detects the behavior measured above.
positions.position_gist: Recommends an inexpensive, fully automatable null-input test as the operational form of the absence comparator, with an exact acceptance criterion that any output produced from signal-free input is a failure.

positions.source_passage: We note that the drafted benchmarking element S.3 treats presenting information with false confidence as a safety failure. We recommend the element be read to include confidence in the premise that input was received at all, and that the absence comparator is the framing under which that failure becomes measurable rather than merely describable.
positions.position_gist: Recommends that benchmarking element S.3 (false confidence as a safety failure) be interpreted to cover false confidence that input was received at all.

positions.source_passage: For this population the fabricated sentence is not a degraded output. It is an utterance entered into the record under the user's name, by a user who cannot contest it.
positions.position_gist: Argues that for nonverbal users, fabricated output creates a distinct harm because the user cannot review or contest a statement attributed to them.
